Appendix B Serving Simulator

We present the concrete cost models used in our roofline-based simulator to instantiate Serve-Cost, Reconfig-Cost, and 𝐓total\mathbf{T}_{\text{total}}. Each GPU type g∈𝐆g\in\mathbf{G} has per-device HBM capacity mgm_{g}, peak FP16 throughput FgF_{g} (FLOPs/s), HBM bandwidth BgB_{g} (bytes/s), PCIe bandwidth PgP_{g} (bytes/s), and νg\nu_{g} GPUs per physical node. Each model MzM_{z} is described by: layers LzL_{z}, hidden dimension HzH_{z}, MLP intermediate dimension IzI_{z}, vocabulary size VzV_{z}, attention heads AzA_{z}, key-value heads Kz≤AzK_{z}\leq A_{z}, per-head dimension dz=Hz/Azd_{z}=H_{z}/A_{z}, and weight precision η\eta bits.

Model Weight Size. The total parameter footprint of MzM_{z} in bytes is:

Wz=[Lz​(3​Hz​Iz+2​Az​Hz​dz+2​Kz​Hz​dz)+2​Hz​Vz]⋅η8W_{z}=\Bigl[L_{z}\bigl(3H_{z}I_{z}+2A_{z}H_{z}d_{z}+2K_{z}H_{z}d_{z}\bigr)+2H_{z}V_{z}\Bigr]\cdot\tfrac{\eta}{8} (2)

where the per-layer terms account for the three MLP projections (3​Hz​Iz3H_{z}I_{z}), the query and output attention projections (2​Az​Hz​dz=2​Hz22A_{z}H_{z}d_{z}=2H_{z}^{2}), the key and value projections (2​Kz​Hz​dz2K_{z}H_{z}d_{z}), and the shared embedding and output-projection matrices (2​Hz​Vz2H_{z}V_{z}).

Roofline-Based Serve Cost. The latency Λ⁡(z,g,t,b,sp,sd)\Lambda(z,g,t,b,s^{p},s^{d}) for a replica group serving MzM_{z} on GPU type gg with TP degree tt and per-replica batch size bb is estimated via the hardware roofline model. For an operation requiring ℱ\mathcal{F} FLOPs and accessing 𝒜\mathcal{A} bytes, the arithmetic intensity is AI=ℱ/𝒜\mathrm{AI}=\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{A} and the ridge point is AI∗=Fg/Bg\mathrm{AI}^{*}=F_{g}/B_{g}. The achieved performance and operation time are:

π⁡(ℱ,𝒜,g)=min⁡(ℱ𝒜⋅Bg,Fg)\displaystyle\pi(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{A},g)=\min\!\left(\frac{\mathcal{F}}{\mathcal{A}}\cdot B_{g},\;F_{g}\right) (3)
Top​(ℱ,𝒜,g)=ℱπ⁡(ℱ,𝒜,g)\displaystyle T^{\mathrm{op}}(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{A},g)=\frac{\mathcal{F}}{\pi(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{A},g)} (4)

The total serve latency sums TopT^{\mathrm{op}} across all transformer sublayers for both the prefill and decode phases, plus the TP all-reduce communication overhead:

Λ⁡(z,g,t,b,sp,sd)\displaystyle\Lambda(z,g,t,b,s^{p},s^{d}) =Tprefill​(z,g,t,b,sp)\displaystyle=T^{\mathrm{prefill}}(z,g,t,b,s^{p}) (5)
+∑k=spsp+sd−1Tdecode(z,g,t,b,k)\displaystyle+\sum_{k=s^{p}}^{s^{p}+s^{d}-1}T^{\mathrm{decode}}(z,g,t,b,k)

where TprefillT^{\mathrm{prefill}} and TdecodeT^{\mathrm{decode}} apply Equation 3 and Equation 4 to each sublayer and add the ring-allreduce time incurred at each of the LzL_{z} transformer layers (two all-reduces per layer: after the attention output projection and after the MLP down-projection):

Tcomm​(z,g,t,b,s)=2​(t−1)t⋅2​Lz⋅Hz⋅b⋅s⋅η8⋅Rg,t−1T^{\mathrm{comm}}(z,g,t,b,s)=\frac{2(t-1)}{t}\cdot 2L_{z}\cdot H_{z}\cdot b\cdot s\cdot\tfrac{\eta}{8}\cdot R_{g,t}^{-1} (6)

where s∈{1,sp}s\in\{1,s^{p}\} is the sequence length for the decode and prefill phases respectively, and Rg,tR_{g,t} is the effective interconnect bandwidth (intra-node when t≤νgt\leq\nu_{g}, cross-node otherwise).

Memory Feasibility. Under TP degree tt, each GPU shard of MzM_{z} holds Wz/tW_{z}/t bytes of model weights. A group (z,g,t,b)(z,g,t,b) is infeasible if the per-shard weight exceeds available device capacity, i.e., OOM issues occur:

Wz/t>θ⋅mgW_{z}/t\;>\;\theta\cdot m_{g} (7)

where θ=0.8\theta=0.8 is a memory utilization threshold reserving headroom for the KV cache. Infeasible groups are assigned a penalty latency Λ∞≫0\Lambda_{\infty}\gg 0; the min-makespan objective then naturally avoids activating them without requiring additional constraints.

Reconfiguration Cost. When consecutive plans σi−1\sigma_{i-1} and σi\sigma_{i} differ for model MzM_{z} — i.e., the (GPU type,TP,count)(\text{GPU type},\,\text{TP},\,\text{count}) tuples changes — the cluster must terminate old replicas and reload new ones via PCIe. Let Δ​𝐌i⊆𝐌\Delta\mathbf{M}_{i}\subseteq\mathbf{M} denote the set of models whose placement changed from σi−1\sigma_{i-1} to σi\sigma_{i}. The reconfiguration cost decomposes as:

Reconfig-Cost​(σi−1,σi)=Tterm​(σi−1,σi)+Tload​(σi)\textsc{Reconfig-Cost}(\sigma_{i-1},\sigma_{i})=T^{\mathrm{term}}(\sigma_{i-1},\sigma_{i})+T^{\mathrm{load}}(\sigma_{i}) (8)

For model MzM_{z} on GPU type gg, the weight transfer time is TP-insensitive (the full model weight is transferred regardless of sharding degree):

τ⁡(z,g)=WzPg⋅cz\tau(z,g)=\frac{W_{z}}{P_{g}}\cdot c_{z} (9)

where cz∈[5.3, 11.5]c_{z}\in[5.3,\,11.5] is a model-size-dependent PCIe bandwidth utilization coefficient (smaller models incur higher per-byte overhead due to PCIe protocol amortization).

The termination cost is the time to drain and evict all changed models from HBM; since different GPU types can terminate concurrently, the bottleneck is the slowest group:

Tterm(σi−1,σi)=maxz∈Δ​𝐌imaxg∈𝐆:σi−1​ deploys ​Mz​ on ​gτ(z,g)T^{\mathrm{term}}(\sigma_{i-1},\sigma_{i})=\max_{z\in\Delta\mathbf{M}_{i}}\;\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}g\in\mathbf{G}:\\ \sigma_{i-1}\text{ deploys }M_{z}\text{ on }g\end{subarray}}\tau(z,g) (10)

The loading cost is the time to transfer new model weights to all target GPU types; since different GPU types load in parallel, the bottleneck is again the slowest:

Tload(σi)=maxg∈𝐆maxz∈𝐌:σi​ deploys ​Mz​ on ​gτ(z,g)T^{\mathrm{load}}(\sigma_{i})=\max_{g\in\mathbf{G}}\;\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\in\mathbf{M}:\\ \sigma_{i}\text{ deploys }M_{z}\text{ on }g\end{subarray}}\tau(z,g) (11)

If σi−1=σi\sigma_{i-1}=\sigma_{i}, both costs are zero.

Appendix C Scheduling Problem Formulation

C.1 Formulation for Case Studies

Scheduling problem formulation. Given a heterogeneous cluster of GPUs, we consider the problem of jointly scheduling multiple models under time-varying workloads. Let 𝐃={d1,…,dK}\mathbf{D}=\{d_{1},\ldots,d_{K}\} denote a set of KK heterogeneous GPU devices, where each device dd has a memory capacity mdm_{d} and distinct compute characteristics. Let 𝐌={M1,…,MZ}\mathbf{M}=\{M_{1},\ldots,M_{Z}\} denote a set of ZZ models. Each model MzM_{z} may serve multiple types of workloads (e.g., inference requests with different input sizes or other requirements), denoted as 𝐖z={wz,1,…,wz,Jz}\mathbf{W}_{z}=\{w_{z,1},\ldots,w_{z,J_{z}}\}.

We consider a discrete time horizon of NN timestamps. At each timestamp i∈{1,…,N}i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}, the system observes a workload demand 𝒲i\mathcal{W}_{i} across all models and workload types. A scheduling plan at timestamp ii is denoted as σi\sigma_{i}, which specifies (i) the assignment of models and workloads to devices, and (ii) the parallel execution configuration, i.e., data, pipeline, or tensor parallelism, for each model. In our context, the data parallelism means the number of inference replicas.

The scheduling plan must satisfy device memory constraints:

Mem-Cumsum​(d,i)≤md,∀d∈𝐃,∀i∈{1,…,N}\textsc{Mem-Cumsum}(d,i)\leq m_{d},\hskip 9.24994pt\forall d\in\mathbf{D},\;\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,N\} (12)

where Mem-Cumsum​(d,i)\textsc{Mem-Cumsum}(d,i) denotes the total memory consumption on device dd at timestamp ii.

Each scheduling plan σi\sigma_{i} incurs four types of costs:

  • •

    Serve-Cost​(σi)\textsc{Serve-Cost}(\sigma_{i}): the serving latency (or execution time) to process workloads at timestamp ii;

  • •

    Reconfig-Cost​(σi−1,σi)\textsc{Reconfig-Cost}(\sigma_{i-1},\sigma_{i}): the reconfiguration overhead due to changes in scheduling decisions across consecutive timestamps, i.e., from σi−1\sigma_{i-1} to σi\sigma_{i};

  • •

    Stale-Cost​(σi)\textsc{Stale-Cost}(\sigma_{i}): the penalty incurred due to stale or delayed serving at timestamp ii;

  • •

    Sched-Cost: the scheduling overhead at the first timestamp.

The end-to-end latency for serving the workload over the time horizon is:

𝐓total=\displaystyle\mathbf{T}_{\text{total}}= Sched-Cost+Serve-Cost​(σ1)\displaystyle\textsc{Sched-Cost}+\textsc{Serve-Cost}(\sigma_{1}) (13)
+∑i=2N[Stale-Cost(σi)\displaystyle+\sum_{i=2}^{N}\Big[\textsc{Stale-Cost}(\sigma_{i})
+Reconfig-Cost​(σi−1,σi)\displaystyle+\textsc{Reconfig-Cost}(\sigma_{i-1},\sigma_{i})
+Serve-Cost(σi)]\displaystyle+\textsc{Serve-Cost}(\sigma_{i})\Big]

Our objective is to find a sequence of scheduling plans 𝝈={σ1,σ2,…,σN}\bm{\sigma}=\{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots,\sigma_{N}\} that minimizes the total trace completion time:

min𝝈\displaystyle\min_{\bm{\sigma}} 𝐓total\displaystyle\mathbf{T}_{\text{total}} (14)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} Mem-Cumsum​(d,i)≤md,\displaystyle\textsc{Mem-Cumsum}(d,i)\leq m_{d},\hskip 9.24994pt
∀d∈𝐃,∀i∈{1,…,N}\displaystyle\forall d\in\mathbf{D},\;\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}

The search space of possible scheduling plans is combinatorial due to (i) heterogeneous device capabilities, (ii) multiple models and workload types, (iii) flexible parallel execution strategies, and (iv) temporal dependencies introduced by reconfiguration costs. Consequently, identifying the optimal sequence of scheduling plans is NP-hard. In practice, we seek efficient heuristic or approximate algorithms to find a near-optimal solution.

C.2 Formulation for Agentic Request

Agentic Request Scheduling Formulation. Given a disaggregated prefill-decode serving cluster, we consider the problem of online scheduling for multi-call agentic workflows. Let 𝐏\mathbf{P} and 𝐐\mathbf{Q} denote the sets of prefill and decode instances, respectively. Each decode instance has a finite token-capacity budget, and different instances may have different serving characteristics.

Let 𝛀={ω1,…,ωB}\mathbf{\Omega}=\{\omega_{1},\ldots,\omega_{B}\} denote a set of workflow requests. Each workflow ω\omega arrives over time and involves a series of LLM calls, each with an input length and an output length. A call becomes schedulable only after all of its predecessor calls have completed, so the scheduler must make decisions under online call revelation.

At each scheduling trigger i∈{1,…,N}i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}, the system observes the currently waiting calls and computes a scheduling plan σi\sigma_{i}. A plan specifies (i) the assignment of each waiting call to a prefill instance and a decode instance, and (ii) the queue order on each instance. The plan must satisfy stage-wise capacity constraints: prefill instances process one call at a time, while decode instances must respect cumulative token-capacity limits.

Each workflow ω\omega has a committed horizon S​L​OωSLO_{\omega} and an actual completion time CωC_{\omega}. The quality of a scheduling policy is measured by the completion ratio Cω/S​L​OωC_{\omega}/SLO_{\omega}, and we use trace-level metrics such as 95t​h95^{th} percentile, 99t​h99^{th} percentile, and mean Cω/S​L​OωC_{\omega}/SLO_{\omega} to evaluate end-to-end performance.

Because scheduling is performed online, each plan σi\sigma_{i} incurs both a scheduling overhead and a serving cost. Let Sched-Cost​(σi)\textsc{Sched-Cost}(\sigma_{i}) denote the planning time at trigger ii, and let Serve-Cost​(σi)\textsc{Serve-Cost}(\sigma_{i}) denote the resulting serving latency contribution. The total trace completion cost is:

𝐓total=∑i=1N[Sched-Cost​(σi)+Serve-Cost​(σi)]\mathbf{T}_{\text{total}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big[\textsc{Sched-Cost}(\sigma_{i})+\textsc{Serve-Cost}(\sigma_{i})\Big] (15)

Our objective is to find a sequence of scheduling plans 𝝈={σ1,σ2,…,σN}\bm{\sigma}=\{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots,\sigma_{N}\} that minimizes end-to-end workflow completion degradation, i.e., improves high-percentile and average Cω/S​L​OωC_{\omega}/SLO_{\omega} while keeping scheduling overhead low enough for online use. The search space is combinatorial due to heterogeneous resources, multi-stage assignment and ordering decisions, token-capacity constraints, and online workflow revelation. Consequently, exact online optimization is expensive, and in practice we seek efficient schedulers that achieve a strong quality-latency trade-off.

In Table 6, we present the initialization configuration of Autopoiesis for the evolutionary process. These configurations are fine-tuned to achieve the optimal performance in the experiments presented in our paper.

Appendix E System Prompts

In this section, we present examples of system prompts we used in Autopoiesis. Across evolutionary iterations, the following prompts are used to guide the LLM to fine-tune the generated program in the next evolutionary iteration.

Search–serving trade-off guidance: For a given workload and heterogeneous cluster, fine-grained exploration of the candidate search space generally yields higher-quality scheduling decisions and lower serving latency. In contrast, coarse-grained exploration tends to produce suboptimal scheduling outcomes and increased serving latency. Accordingly, prompts should be carefully designed to guide the LLM in balancing search granularity against scheduling quality. Our detailed prompt message for this guidance is shown in prompt message episode 1.

Reconfiguration and serving trade-off guidance: More comprehensive reconfiguration generally results in lower serving latency but incurs higher reconfiguration costs. Conversely, less extensive reconfiguration tends to reduce reconfiguration costs at the expense of increased serving latency. Therefore, we guide the LLM to balance the trade-off between reconfiguration cost and serving latency. The detailed prompt message is presented in prompt message episode 2.

Prompt Message Episode 1: Search Granularity vs. Scheduling Efficiency max_batch_per_replica controls how finely the ILP searches over batch sizes for each model. It represents a fundamental search granularity vs. scheduling efficiency trade-off — there is no universally correct value; the right choice depends on the model’s memory footprint and workload characteristics. Larger cap →\rightarrow fine-grained search, lower scheduling efficiency: • More batch-size candidates →\rightarrow larger ILP →\rightarrow slower solve time. • The scheduler can find placements that match the workload’s total_batch more precisely (e.g., a replica batch of 96 vs. only 64), potentially reducing latency. • Each extra candidate adds integer and binary variables, making the solver (e.g., CBC) work harder. Smaller cap →\rightarrow coarse-grained search, higher scheduling efficiency: • Fewer candidates →\rightarrow smaller ILP →\rightarrow faster solve time. • The scheduler selects from a coarser set of batch sizes and may slightly over- or under-shoot the ideal per-replica load. • For models where latency is relatively insensitive to batch size in the relevant range, the quality loss is negligible while the speed gain is significant. Key Insight: Some models need fine-grained search, others do not. • Models with large total_batch and flat latency-vs-batch curves benefit from finer granularity, enabling better packing. • Memory-constrained models have few feasible batch sizes regardless of the cap — increasing it introduces infeasible (OOM) candidates, adding overhead without benefit. • Models with steep latency-vs-batch curves benefit from a moderate cap that captures the efficient region without exploring far into OOM. Additional Insight: Raising the cap for small models can reduce the number of required replicas, thereby freeing GPUs for larger models. For example, if a small model has total_batch = 256 and the cap is set to 256, only one replica is required (versus 8 replicas at cap = 32), freeing 7 GPUs that can be allocated to larger models to reduce latency. Implementation Guidance: The initial program uses a uniform cap (defined in workloads.py, which is fixed), providing a safe and conservative baseline. LLM-evolved programs should instead choose per-model caps within their EVOLVE-BLOCKS based on model characteristics (e.g., weight size, memory footprint, and typical batch sizes). These caps can be different across timestamps. Inspect workloads.py to understand the total_batch range for each model across timestamps.
Prompt Message Episode 2: The Reconfiguration Trade-off — When to Reschedule The total cost for one timestamp is: e2e=ilp solve time+serving latency+reconfig cost\text{e2e}=\text{ilp solve time}+\text{serving latency}+\text{reconfig cost} (16) A new schedule that saves Δ\Delta seconds of serving and scheduling latency is only worthwhile if: Δ>reconfig cost\Delta>\text{reconfig cost} (17) Concrete Trade-off Examples Example A — Reschedule pays off: Suppose at t​s0ts_{0} you have a large model on fast GPUs with serving latency 20002000 ms. Appendix F Additional Case Study

F.1 Scheduling Algorithm Optimization

Setup. We consider a real-world LLM serving deployment at the Swiss AI Center [34], where a heterogeneous GPU cluster serves multiple LLMs under dynamic workloads. In this scenario, we isolate the scheduling algorithm as the optimization target: Given a fixed workload snapshot and cluster configuration, the objective is to evolve a scheduling algorithm that produces serving plans (i.e., workload assignments, resource allocations, and parallelism strategies) of equivalent quality to a ILP-based [43] scheduling algorithm while minimizing plan generation time.

Traces. We use two workload snapshots from Swiss AI Center [34], each representing a distinct workload and cluster configuration. Detailed problem formulation and trace information are shown in Appendix C and Appendix H.

Results analysis. The baseline ILP-based scheduler requires an average of 120s per invocation across the two traces. The evolved scheduling algorithm reduces this to 9s, a 13×13{\times} speedup, with less than 3% degradation in plan quality. Examining the evolved code reveals complementary modifications across multiple algorithmic layers: Search space reduction through curated candidate selection, tighter LP relaxation via per-variable bounds, valid inequalities encoding domain-specific constraints, strengthened secondary objectives for better solution guidance, and optimized solver parameters. A detailed comparison of the baseline and evolved code is provided in Appendix G.

Insight 5: Synthesis discovers deployment-tailored algorithmic optimizations. Rather than converging on a single type of improvement, the synthesis workflow discovers complementary optimizations spanning problem formulation, domain knowledge injection, objective shaping, and solver configuration. Crucially, these optimizations are tailored to the specific workload and cluster configuration and would shift under different deployment conditions, highlighting the value of LLM-driven program synthesis over manual algorithm tuning.

Appendix G Evolved Scheduling Algorithm Analysis

In this section, we analyze the details of the code generated by LLMs. The LLM-driven improvements include smarter batch selection, per-variable bounds, stronger weighted objective, and solver-specific tuning. These enhancements significantly reduce ILP solve time while preserving the optimal makespan, highlighting the value of integrating domain knowledge with automated code refinement. The details are discussed below.

Optimization on batch candidate selection. In the LLM-generated program, the selection of batch candidates was refined compared to the naive exhaustive search employed in the initial program, which served as the starting point for the LLM’s evolutionary improvements. Instead of traversing all possible batch sizes, the LLM generates a curated set of candidates, combining powers of 2, divisors of the total batch size, and manually selected sweet spots. Specifically, the resulting batch candidates are designed to balance computational efficiency and hardware utilization. The detailed batch candidates are shown as follows:

Batch Candidates\displaystyle\text{Batch Candidates} ={1,2,3,4,6}∪{2k∣k=2,…,6}\displaystyle=\{1,2,3,4,6\}\;\cup\;\{2^{k}\mid k=2,\dots,6\}\; (18)
∪{20,24,28,32,40,48}\displaystyle\cup\;\{20,24,28,32,40,48\}

Optimization on parallel strategy. The LLM incorporates a domain-specific constraint for large models (e.g., 70B), requiring a sufficiently high tensor parallelism degree, specifically enforcing t≥4t\geq 4. This ensures that large models are allocated adequate parallel resources, preventing inefficient configurations that often result in out-of-memory errors.

Optimizations on the objective function and formulation. To enhance the efficiency of the ILP solver, the LLM-generated code incorporates two key optimizations: (i) tighter per-variable Big-M bounds, which strengthen the LP relaxation, and (ii) a weighted objective, which provides improved guidance when multiple solutions share the same makespan. The notations used below are defined in Table 5.

  • •

    Per-variable Big-M bounds. For model type zz, GPU type gg, tensor-paralel degree tt, and batch size bb, the standard indicator constraint linking nz,g,t,bn_{z,g,t,b} and yz,g,t,by_{z,g,t,b} is: nz,g,t,b≤M⋅yz,g,t,bn_{z,g,t,b}\leq M\cdot y_{z,g,t,b}, where MM is a sufficiently large constant; a naive formulation uses a single global bound M=maxg∈𝐆⁡κgM=\max_{g\in\mathbf{G}}\kappa_{g}, which is overly loose for most variables.

    Instead, the LLM defines a variable-specific bound for each possible tuple (z,g,t,b)(z,g,t,b):

    Mz,g,t,b\displaystyle M_{z,g,t,b} =min⁡(⌊κgt⌋,⌈λzb⌉)\displaystyle=\min\Bigg(\left\lfloor\frac{\kappa_{g}}{t}\right\rfloor,\left\lceil\frac{\lambda_{z}}{b}\right\rceil\Bigg) (19)

    The indicator constraint becomes:

    nz,g,t,b≤Mz,g,t,b⋅yz,g,t,bn_{z,g,t,b}\leq M_{z,g,t,b}\cdot y_{z,g,t,b} (20)

    Here, ⌊κgt⌋\left\lfloor\frac{\kappa_{g}}{t}\right\rfloor bounds the number of replicas by available GPU capacity, ⌈λzb⌉\left\lceil\frac{\lambda_{z}}{b}\right\rceil bounds the number of replicas required to cover the workload. The term per-variable emphasizes that each decision variable nz,g,t,bn_{z,g,t,b} has its own tight upper bound, instead of sharing a single global constant. This significantly tightens the LP relaxation: when yz,g,t,by_{z,g,t,b} takes fractional values, the feasible range of nz,g,t,bn_{z,g,t,b} is correspondingly restricted. As a result, the solver obtains stronger bounds and can prune the branch-and-bound search tree more effectively.

  • •

    Weighted objective. The primary objective is to minimize the global makespan:

    min⁡Tbalanced,s.t. ​Tbalanced≥Lz,∀z∈𝐌\min\;T_{\text{balanced}},\hskip 9.24994pt\text{s.t. }T_{\text{balanced}}\geq L_{z},\hskip 9.24994pt\forall z\in\mathbf{M} (21)

    The variable LzL_{z} is defined through:

    Lz≥Λz,g,t,b⋅yz,g,t,b,∀g∈𝐆,t∈𝒯g,b∈ℬzL_{z}\geq\Lambda_{z,g,t,b}\cdot y_{z,g,t,b},\hskip 9.24994pt\forall g\in\mathbf{G},\;t\in\mathcal{T}_{g},\;b\in\mathcal{B}_{z} (22)

    LzL_{z} captures the completion latency of model MzM_{z}, determined by its slowest active replica group. While minimizing TbalancedT_{\text{balanced}} ensures fairness across models, multiple solutions may achieve the same optimal makespan but differ in individual model latencies. To guide the solver toward better practical solutions, the LLM introduces a weighted objective (zz indexes models in increasing order of size, i.e., a larger zz corresponds to a larger LLM):

    Weighted Obj=ϵ​∑z∈𝐌(1.0+0.5⋅z)​Lz,ϵ=0.05\text{Weighted Obj}=\epsilon\sum_{z\in\mathbf{M}}\big(1.0+0.5\cdot z\big)\,L_{z},\hskip 9.24994pt\epsilon=0.05 (23)

    This strategy assigns larger weights to larger LLMs, encouraging the solver to reduce their latency when possible. Compared to an unweighted and very small secondary term, this stronger formulation provides a clearer optimization signal, helping the solver distinguish between solutions with identical makespan and converge faster to high-quality solutions.

Optimization on ILP solver. The ILP solver, i.e., CBC solver, was carefully tuned by the LLM. We summarize the details in Table 7. These settings directly accelerate ILP convergence while maintaining solution quality within a negligible 0.3% optimality gap.

Appendix H Trace Information

H.1 Trace Information for the Motivation Section

We present two motivating traces using Qwen2.5 models (1.5B–72B). In the heavy-dominant phase (H), small models (1.5B/3B/7B) serve low batch sizes (64/64/64) with 256-token prefill sequence length and short decode sequence lengths (2048/1536/3072 tokens), while large models (14B/32B/72B) carry high batch loads (384/256/128) with 512-token prefill length and long decode sequence lengths (8192/6144/5120 tokens); in the light-dominant phase (L), small models dominate (960/480/288 batch, 256-token prefill sequence length, 4096/3072/6144-token decoding sequence length), while large models are minimally loaded (64/32/16 batch, 256-token prefill sequence length, 2048/1536/1280-token decoding sequence length).

Trace for Figure 2 (left). As shown in Table 8, this 3-timestamp trace features two abrupt phase transitions, demonstrating the scheduler’s need for rapid response. The system starts in a heavy-dominant phase (ts0), abruptly shifts to a light-dominant phase (ts1), and reverts to heavy-dominant at ts2. Each transition dramatically redistributes load across all model sizes.

Trace for Figure 2 (right). As shown in Table 9, this 5-timestamp trace hybridizes stable and volatile behavior. The workload begins in a light-dominant phase with minor perturbations (ts0–ts1), undergoes one abrupt shift to the heavy-dominant phase at ts2, and then stabilizes with minor perturbations (ts3–ts4). This demonstrates that even predominantly stable workloads benefit from adaptive rescheduling at shift boundaries.

Stable workload in §8.1. We consider a production workload consisting of 10 timestamps (ts0–ts9) and three Qwen2.5 model sizes (1.5B, 3B, and 7B), where batch sizes and sequence lengths remain mostly stable with occasional variations. The prefill length is fixed at 256 tokens for all models throughout. The decoding lengths are 4096, 3072, and 6144 tokens for the 1.5B, 3B, and 7B models, respectively. H.3 Trace Information for the Main Experiments

Across the main experiments, we use phase labels to indicate the dominant token-shape characteristic of each workload segment. A prefill-heavy phase has relatively long input sequences and short output sequences; a decode-heavy phase has relatively short input sequences and long output sequences; a balanced-short phase has short inputs and short outputs; and a stable-mixed or stable-decode-heavy phase denotes a later stable period whose token-shape profile remains similar across consecutive timestamps.

DistServe. The DistServe evaluation uses two traces sampled from ShareGPT and LongBench, respectively. We divide each trace into six workload phases, where each timestamp corresponds to the beginning of a workload phase. Each of the six ShareGPT phases contains 51205120 requests, and each LongBench phase contains 17281728 requests. Specifically, the ShareGPT trace contains one prefill-heavy phase, one decode-heavy phase, one short balanced phase, and then three stable mixed phases. The LongBench trace contains two prefill-heavy phases, one decode-heavy transition phase, and then three stable decode-heavy phases. The phase-wise mean token-shape profiles are listed in Table 14.

HexGen. The HexGen evaluation uses the same phase-wise token-shape profiles as DistServe. The difference is workload intensity: each workload phase in ShareGPT trace contains 9216 requests, and each workload phase in LongBench contains 3110 requests. Thus, the prefill and decode lengths in Table 14 remain unchanged, while the effective workload size is scaled up.

SpotServe. This evaluation uses two MAF-derived traces, each combining hidden workload-pattern changes with a time-varying elastic cluster-size schedule. Both traces are extracted from a real Azure Functions application window and then mapped into an elastic cluster schedule ranging from 2424 to 6464 GPUs. In the current construction, the two traces share the same planner-visible cluster schedule. Table 15 lists the hidden workload phases, and Table 16 lists the shared cluster-size schedule.

Appendix I Discussion and Limitation

LLM API stability and cost. The evolutionary process relies on LLM API calls for candidate mutation, making it sensitive to API availability and latency. Unstable API endpoints can stall individual evolution cycles, prolonging the time before an improved policy is deployed. Additionally, LLM inference introduces non-trivial monetary cost—commercial APIs such as Claude charge considerable per-token fees that may be prohibitive for continuous evolution in production. To mitigate this, Autopoiesis is designed to be model-agnostic: Our current deployment uses open-source models, making operational cost substantially more manageable while maintaining competitive synthesis quality. This also demonstrates that our approach does not rely on frontier-class closed-source LLMs to be effective.

LLM capability and hallucination. The quality of evolved policies is inherently bounded by the code-generation capability of the underlying LLM. Stronger models generally produce more effective mutations and converge faster, while weaker models may require more iterations. Moreover, LLM hallucinations can generate syntactically valid but semantically incorrect policies. Our multi-level timeout hierarchy (§6) and automated evaluation (§5.3) serve as safeguards by discarding candidates that crash, diverge, or degrade fitness, but hallucination rates at production scale remain a factor that influences evolution efficiency.

Snapshot window configuration. The length of the runtime trace snapshot presents a trade-off: An overly long window aggregates information across multiple workload regimes, diluting the signal of the current operating state and potentially producing policies optimized for an averaged rather than present condition. Conversely, an overly short window may be dominated by transient fluctuations, causing the evolved policy to overfit to momentary noise rather than sustained trends. In our current implementation, the window size is a configurable parameter; adaptive window sizing based on detected workload volatility is a promising direction for future work.

Evolution time overhead. Each evolution cycle incurs wall-clock time for candidate generation, evaluation, and selection. We address this through two mechanisms: (i) Warm-start re-evolution (§6), which reduces convergence time by up to 83% when consecutive snapshots reflect gradual shifts, and (ii) parallel candidate evaluation, which accelerates the evaluation stage by up to 8×\times with 10×\times more concurrent CPU threads. Further reduction through speculative evaluation or early termination of unpromising candidates remains an avenue for future optimization.

Adaptability to diverse serving objectives. Our execution model and evaluator are formulated around end-to-end trace completion time, but this choice is not fundamental to the architecture. The policy interface (should_reschedule and schedule) and the three-phase interval structure remain unchanged regardless of the objective. To optimize for alternative metrics such as P95 latency or SLO attainment, only the evaluator’s aggregation logic needs modification: Instead of summing per-interval costs into Ttotal\text{T}_{\text{total}}, the simulator tracks per-request latency across the trace replay and the evaluator computes the target metric (e.g., the 95th-percentile latency or the fraction of requests meeting a latency threshold) as the scalar fitness score. Since the synthesis workflow treats the fitness score as a black-box scalar, this substitution requires no changes to the mutation, selection, or deployment mechanisms, enabling Autopoiesis to optimize for the serving metric most relevant to a given deployment scenario.

Appendix J Extended Related Work

LLM serving systems. Recent works have proposed several systems and methods for highly efficient LLM serving [44, 45, 46, 47, 35, 19, 12, 48, 49, 50, 51]. AlpaServe [4] optimizes system service level objectives (SLOs) by utilizing data and model parallelism; DistServe [6] and Splitwise [52] split the prefill and decoding phases onto separate GPUs to eliminate interference between them; SarathiServe [3] optimizes request batching through prefill chunking to mitigate interference between the prefill and decoding stages; vLLM [14] introduces PagedAttention for efficient memory management, enabling higher batch sizes and improved throughput; FastServe [53] employs a preemptive scheduling mechanism that prioritizes shorter jobs to minimize job completion time. These works primarily focus on improving serving performance through techniques such as batching optimization, phase separation, and memory management. In contrast, our work focuses on deployment scheduling with heterogeneous LLMs and GPU types to achieve cost-efficient LLM serving.

Parallelism strategies. Training and serving LLMs that exceed the memory capacity of a single GPU requires a combination of parallelism strategies. Data parallelism replicates the full model across devices and partitions training batches or distributes inference requests among replicas, scaling throughput but requiring each device to hold the entire model [4]. Tensor parallelism partitions individual operations — such as the large matrix multiplications in attention and feed-forward layers — across devices within a node, reducing per-GPU memory usage and per-step or per-request latency at the cost of frequent all-reduce communication [26, 54]. Pipeline parallelism divides the model into sequential stages across devices, enabling larger models to be trained or served by overlapping the execution of different micro-batches across stages, though it introduces pipeline bubbles and increased latency [27]. Hybrid parallelism combines all three approaches to efficiently scale massive models while jointly balancing latency, throughput, and memory constraints [55, 56, 57, 58].
